name: An inferred carpenter's household (north division)
head: inf_carpenter_north_05

arrival.note: NOT AN ARRIVAL, A BOUND. Nothing dates a hypothesised household, and a year would be a claim nobody made. `not_later_than` the scene date states the only thing the inference carries: the town's need is measured on 1 July 1835, so the household is posited as being here by then and at no stated time before it.

party_size_on_arrival.note: Not claimed. The layer infers households, not families: the person entries here are the ones the trade argument requires and nothing counts wives or children, because counting them would multiply a hypothesis by an invention.

origin.note: Not claimed. Where a hypothesised resident came from is unknowable by construction, and the documented layer's origins (Vermont, Washington, Ann Arbor) are evidence about those men and not a distribution to sample from.

reason_for_coming.note: Not claimed for the person. The reason the HOUSEHOLD is in the dataset is the trade argument in research_note, which is a statement about the town and not about a motive.

lives_at.note: THE HOUSEHOLD IS HOUSED, WHICH IS THE POINT OF THE LAYER. recon_1835_north_d3_002 is an anonymous inferred roof already standing on the plat, adopted rather than duplicated: its existence, position and footprint stay conjectural and the adoption adds only the occupant argument. Which roof of the right family and district a hypothesised household occupies is not evidence about that roof; the household needed a dwelling and the programme assigned it one.

works_at.note: recon_1835_north_w2_005 is an anonymous inferred roof already standing on the plat, adopted rather than duplicated: its existence, position and footprint stay conjectural and the adoption adds only the occupant argument. The workplace is assigned from the reconstruction schedule's workshop and store families for this trade.

present_on_scene_date.note: Presence on the scene date IS the hypothesis: this household exists in the dataset because the town of 1 July 1835 demonstrably needed households of this trade. It is not a finding about anybody's whereabouts.

persons.name: A carpenter (inferred resident, unnamed)

occupation.note: THE TRADE THE TOWN NEEDED MOST AND THE ONE THE DOCUMENTED LAYER UNDER-COUNTS WORST. The 1835 town census counts 3,265 people in 398 dwellings; Andreas's roster of the fall of 1833 describes a settlement of a few dozen buildings, and the reconstruction specification puts 665 roofs on the ground by July 1835. Several hundred of those roofs went up inside eighteen months. Even at a crew of three raising a one-room frame cottage in three weeks, that is on the order of forty carpenter-years of work in a year and a half. Andreas names four carpenters and one ship carpenter in the whole of the 1833 town. Ten carpenter households are inferred against the schedule's eight W2 carpenter-or-joiner shops, because a house carpenter worked on the frame in the street and not in a shop: the shop count is a floor under the trade, not a measure of it.

persons.note: HYPOTHESISED, AND NOT A PERSON. No source names this resident and none is claimed to: the record asserts that a town of 3,265 people in 398 dwellings held at least this many households of this trade, and asserts nothing whatever about any individual. The name field carries a designation because inventing a surname would make this record indistinguishable at a glance from the documented layer beside it. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). research_note: INFERRED HOUSEHOLD - fifth of 10 carpenter households in this layer, in the north division. THE TRADE THE TOWN NEEDED MOST AND THE ONE THE DOCUMENTED LAYER UNDER-COUNTS WORST. The 1835 town census counts 3,265 people in 398 dwellings; Andreas's roster of the fall of 1833 describes a settlement of a few dozen buildings, and the reconstruction specification puts 665 roofs on the ground by July 1835. Several hundred of those roofs went up inside eighteen months. Even at a crew of three raising a one-room frame cottage in three weeks, that is on the order of forty carpenter-years of work in a year and a half. Andreas names four carpenters and one ship carpenter in the whole of the 1833 town. Ten carpenter households are inferred against the schedule's eight W2 carpenter-or-joiner shops, because a house carpenter worked on the frame in the street and not in a shop: the shop count is a floor under the trade, not a measure of it. METHOD: the count comes from the occupation census in data/reconstruction/1835_inferred_household_programme.json, which calibrates every trade against three things this project already holds - the 1835 town census (3,265 people, 398 dwellings), Andreas's roster of the fall of 1833 (about fifty named people, most with a trade, in a settlement of some 350), and the reconstruction specification's roof schedule, whose workshop and store family targets are treated as the ceiling on a trade rather than as its measure. Every count is stated NET of the documented layer: this dataset infers a tradesman only where it cannot name one.
